lead: A computer is a set of blocks that move data and instructions. The CPU does arithmetic and logic, holds a few values in registers, and controls the order of work. Memory stores instructions and data. Input and output devices connect the computer to the world. They all share three buses: address, data and control. The address bus selects a location, the data bus carries the bits, and the control bus says read or write. This organization appears in laptops, phones, washing machines and ATMs.
prereq: You need: processor terms from Chapter 1.1 and binary powers such as 210 = 1024 and 216 = 65536.

blocks.text: The CPU is the part that executes instructions. The arithmetic logic unit (ALU) adds, subtracts, ANDs, ORs and compares binary numbers. Registers are small, fast storage inside the CPU. A general-purpose processor has registers for operands, a program counter (PC) that holds the address of the next instruction, and an instruction register (IR) that holds the instruction being decoded. Flags are single bits that record the result of the last operation, for example zero, carry or sign. The control unit reads the opcode in the IR and sends timed signals to the ALU, registers and buses. It decides which register drives the internal bus, which ALU operation runs, and when memory is read or written. The data path is the set of registers, ALU and internal buses that carry operands and results. The control path is the control unit and its signal lines that tell the data path what to do. Data flows along the data path; control flows along the control path. This block diagram is what some syllabi call a general purpose processor or computer organization block diagram.

A bus is a group of wires that many units share. The address bus carries the address of the memory location or I/O port. It is usually driven by the CPU and is unidirectional. If the address bus has n lines, the CPU can select 2n distinct addresses. This number is the address space. The data bus carries the actual bits. If it has m lines, one bus cycle moves m bits. An 8-bit data bus moves one byte per cycle; a 16-bit bus moves two bytes. The data bus is bidirectional, because data flows from CPU to memory or device on a write and from memory or device to CPU on a read. The control bus carries timing and command signals: read, write, clock, interrupt request and reset. A read cycle works in a fixed order. The CPU places a valid address on the address bus. It asserts the read control line. Memory or the I/O device places data on the data bus. The CPU samples the data near the end of the cycle. A write cycle is similar, but the CPU puts data on the data bus and asserts write. The address must stay valid until the transfer finishes. Bus width matters: address width sets how much memory you can reach, and data width sets how many bits move at once. Do not mix the two. The 8085 and 8086 bus signals and machine cycles are covered in Unit 2.

blocks.where: N is the number of addressable locations and n is the number of address lines.

blocks.text: Memory holds instructions and data in numbered locations. Each location has an address. Memory-mapped I/O gives an I/O device registers that look like memory locations. The CPU uses ordinary load and store instructions to read or write them. Isolated I/O keeps a separate I/O address space. The CPU uses special instructions such as IN and OUT, and the control bus carries an extra signal to choose I/O instead of memory. Isolated I/O protects memory addresses but needs extra instructions. An I/O port is the register or connection point through which the CPU talks to a device. A simple keyboard port may have a data register and a status bit. In polling, the CPU repeatedly reads the status bit until it says ready, then reads the data. Polling is simple but wastes CPU time. In interrupt operation, the device raises an interrupt request line when it is ready. The CPU finishes the current instruction, saves its state, and jumps to a short service routine. The routine reads or writes the device and returns. Both methods use the same buses; only the control sequence changes. Memory types and chip organization are in Chapter 1.5.

figure.caption: The CPU drives the bus system; memory and I/O devices respond only when selected. Notice that all addresses, data and control signals pass through the same three bus groups.

spec.aria: A CPU connects through a bus system carrying address, data and control signals to memory and to input and output devices.

examples.question: A simple computer has 16 address lines and 8 data lines. Find its address space in bytes and the number of bytes it can transfer in one bus cycle. It uses an 8 KB ROM and a 2 KB RAM; how many address lines does each need?
steps: Address space = 2<sup>16</sup> locations = 65536 locations. Each location holds one byte, so the address space is 65536 bytes = 64 KB.
Data bus width = 8 bits = 1 byte, so one bus cycle transfers 1 byte.
ROM size = 8 KB = 8 × 1024 = 8192 bytes = 2<sup>13</sup> bytes, so the ROM needs 13 address lines.
RAM size = 2 KB = 2 × 1024 = 2048 bytes = 2<sup>11</sup> bytes, so the RAM needs 11 address lines.
examples.answer: Address space is 65536 bytes (64 KB); one bus cycle transfers 1 byte; the 8 KB ROM needs 13 address lines and the 2 KB RAM needs 11 address lines.
examples.check:
import math
addr_lines = 16
data_lines = 8
address_space = 2 ** addr_lines
bytes_per_cycle = data_lines // 8
rom_bytes = 8 * 1024
ram_bytes = 2 * 1024
rom_lines = int(math.log2(rom_bytes))
ram_lines = int(math.log2(ram_bytes))
print(address_space)
print(bytes_per_cycle)
print(rom_lines)
print(ram_lines)

traps: Address bus width is not data bus width. 16 address lines give 2¹⁶ = 65536 addresses (64 KB), not 16 KB.
A byte is 8 bits. A data bus of 8 lines moves 1 byte per cycle, not 8 bytes.
Memory-mapped I/O uses normal memory instructions; isolated I/O uses special IN/OUT instructions and a separate I/O address space.
In a read cycle the CPU samples data after the read strobe; in a write cycle the CPU drives data before the write strobe. Do not swap them.
An address space of 2ⁿ bytes needs n address lines only when each address selects one byte. Word-addressed memory changes the byte count.

quiz.q: Name the three buses in a computer and state what each carries.
quiz.a: Address bus carries the location address; data bus carries the bits being moved; control bus carries read, write, clock and interrupt signals.

quiz.q: What do the program counter and instruction register hold?
quiz.a: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction. The instruction register holds the instruction currently being decoded.

quiz.q: Why is the address bus usually unidirectional?
quiz.a: The CPU is normally the master that selects memory or I/O. It drives the address out, and memory or I/O devices only decode it. A shared bidirectional address bus would need extra control and arbitration.

quiz.q: A CPU has 12 address lines and 16 data lines. Find its address space in bytes and the number of bytes it transfers per bus cycle.
quiz.a: Address space = 2¹² = 4096 bytes. Data bus = 16 bits = 2 bytes per bus cycle.

quiz.q: A system has 32 KB ROM and 8 KB RAM. How many address lines does each need?
quiz.a: 32 KB = 32768 bytes = 2¹⁵, so 15 address lines. 8 KB = 8192 bytes = 2¹³, so 13 address lines.

quiz.q: A system has a 64 KB address space, 32 KB ROM and 8 KB RAM. Can both fit? Explain the address-line count.
quiz.a: Yes. 32 KB needs 15 lines and 8 KB needs 13 lines. Total memory is 40 KB, which is less than 64 KB. The remaining 24 KB can be unused or used by I/O and expansion.

quiz.q: Compare memory-mapped I/O and isolated I/O.
quiz.a: Memory-mapped I/O places device registers in the memory address space and uses ordinary load/store instructions. Isolated I/O uses a separate I/O address space and special IN/OUT instructions.

quiz.q: Why does a wider data bus improve throughput for large data transfers?
quiz.a: A wider bus moves more bits per bus cycle. For the same number of bytes, fewer bus cycles are needed, so transfer time falls when memory and devices can supply the wider words.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern chips use on-chip buses and crossbars, not one shared bus; ARM systems often use AXI or AHB for high-speed memory-mapped I/O. Search for AMBA AXI, memory-mapped I/O, bus arbitration and DMA. The same ideas appear in system-on-chip design, where CPU, GPU, memory controller and peripherals share address and data paths.
